mainTopic: The end of the story of the wise captives, teachings on the פסוקים of איכה, and who made the משנה's list of those with no share in עולם הבא.
overview: This amud opens with the end of a story about two Jewish captives. They correctly figure out details about a camel far ahead of them, and their captor checks, honors them and sets them free. The גמרא then goes back to explaining the פסוקים of איכה. The doubled weeping stands for the two בתי המקדש, and 'at night' points to the night ישראל cried over the מרגלים. That night was תשעה באב, so it became a day of crying for all generations. Several other meanings of 'at night' follow, along with the story of רבן גמליאל and his grieving neighbor. More teachings of רבא in the name of רבי יוחנן explain further phrases, including why ירושלים was not treated with favoritism compared to סדום: it suffered a terrible famine that סדום never knew. Finally the גמרא returns to the משנה's list of those with no share in עולם הבא. The אנשי כנסת הגדולה made the list and were stopped by heaven from adding שלמה. The דורשי רשומות then argue that all of those listed do come to עולם הבא, a reading that continues on the next amud.

steps.title: A captive describes a camel he cannot see
steps.stepSummary: One captive tells the other surprising details about a camel walking ahead of them.
steps.simpleTranslation: One of the captives said to the other: The camel walking ahead of us is blind in one eye. It carries two flasks, one of wine and one of oil. Two people are leading it, one a ישראל and one a גוי.
steps.whatsHappening: In the middle of the story, one captive makes a list of claims about a camel that is out of sight. This sets up the captor's question in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The captive gives three separate details: the camel's eye, what it is carrying, and who is leading it. None of these can be seen directly, so the reader is meant to wonder how he knows. The answer comes in step 3.

keyTerms.meaning: Skin flasks used to carry liquids
The ones leading or driving (the animal)

phrases.english: One of them said to his friend:
The camel that is walking ahead of us
is blind in one of its eyes,
and it is loaded with two flasks,

phrases.aramaic: אַחַת שֶׁל יַיִן וְאַחַת שֶׁל שֶׁמֶן,
phrases.english: one of wine and one of oil,
and two people are leading it,
one a Jew and one a gentile.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר לוֹ אֶחָד מֵהֶם לַחֲבֵירוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues a story that began earlier on the daf.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The captive claims three hidden facts about the camel ahead.

steps.title: The captor asks how they know
steps.stepSummary: The captor, שבאי, scolds the captives and demands to know how they could know these things.
steps.simpleTranslation: The captor said to them: Stiff-necked people! How do you know this?
steps.whatsHappening: The captor challenges the captives to explain how they know what they cannot see. This sets up their explanation in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Calling them 'stiff-necked' shows he thinks they are just making things up. His question gives them the opening to show that their claims come from careful observation.

keyTerms.meaning: Stiff-necked people, an insult meaning stubborn

phrases.english: The captor said to them:
phrases.notes: שבאי means 'the captor.' Some versions don't have this word; the corrected wording adds it.

phrases.english: Stiff-necked people!
From where do you know?

steps.triggerLanguage: מֵאֵין אַתֶּם יוֹדְעִין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions the claims made in step 1.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: How the captives could know details about a camel they cannot see.

steps.title: The captives explain each clue
steps.stepSummary: The captives show that each detail came from signs left on the road.
steps.simpleTranslation: They said: We know the camel is half-blind from the grass along the road. It eats on the side it can see and leaves the other side alone. We know about the wine and the oil because wine drips and sinks into the ground, while oil drips and floats on top. We know about the two leaders because the גוי relieved himself right on the road, while the ישראל went off to the side.
steps.whatsHappening: The captives answer the captor's question by explaining, one by one, the clue behind each of their three claims.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each claim from step 1 now gets its own proof. Grass is eaten on only one side, so the camel sees on only one side. The drips behave differently, so two different liquids are being carried. Two kinds of droppings in two places show two different people. The last clue also shows the modesty of a ישראל.

phrases.english: They said to him:
The camel: from the grass in front of it,
on the side that it sees, it eats,
on the side that it does not see, it does not eat.
And it is loaded with two flasks,

phrases.aramaic: אַחַת שֶׁל יַיִן וְאַחַת שֶׁל שֶׁמֶן;
phrases.english: one of wine and one of oil;
the wine drips and sinks in,
and the oil drips and floats.
And two people are leading it,
one a gentile and one a Jew;
the gentile relieves himself on the road,
and the Jew relieves himself off to the sides.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמְרוּ לוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the captor's question from step 2.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Each claim is based on a sign left on the road: grass eaten on one side only, two kinds of drips, and droppings in two different places.

steps.title: The captor checks, honors them, and frees them
steps.stepSummary: The captor confirms their claims, throws them a feast, praises God for the wisdom of אברהם's children, and sends them home.
steps.simpleTranslation: He chased after the camel and found everything just as they said. He came back, kissed them on their heads, brought them to his house, and made them a great feast. He danced before them and said: Blessed is the One who chose the children of אברהם and gave them some of His wisdom. Wherever they go, they become princes to their masters. Then he released them, and they went home in peace.
steps.whatsHappening: The story ends. The captor checks the captives' claims, finds them true, and rewards them with honor and freedom.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The captor started out calling them 'stiff-necked' and ends up dancing before them. Checking the facts changed his mind completely. His blessing names the lesson: God gave wisdom to the children of אברהם, and it raises them up even when they are captives.
steps.whatToRemember: The captives' wisdom turned an enemy who mocked them into someone who honored them and set them free.

phrases.english: He chased after them
phrases.notes: "Them" here means the camel and its two drivers.

phrases.english: and found it as they had said.
He came and kissed them on their heads,
and brought them to his house
and made them a great feast.
And he was dancing before them and said:
Blessed is the One who chose the offspring of Abraham
and gave them from His wisdom,
and in every place that they go
they become princes to their masters.
And he released them, and they went to their homes in peace.
phrases.notes: Some versions don't have the word in square brackets; the corrected wording adds it.

steps.triggerLanguage: רָדַף אַחֲרֵיהֶם וּמָצָא כְּדִבְרֵיהֶם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Confirms the answer from step 3 and closes the story.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The captives' claims prove true. The captor honors them, praises the God-given wisdom of אברהם's children, and frees them.

steps.title: Why does the פסוק double the word for weeping?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא goes back to the פסוקים of איכה and asks why the word for weeping is written twice.
steps.simpleTranslation: The פסוק says 'בָּכֹה תִבְכֶּה בַּלַּיְלָה', 'she weeps, weeps, at night.' Why does it mention two weepings?
steps.whatsHappening: The story is over, and the גמרא goes back to explaining the פסוקים of איכה. It asks about an extra word, which sets up רבה's answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The Hebrew doubles the verb (בָּכֹה תִבְכֶּה). The גמרא treats the doubling as a hint to two separate weepings and asks what each one is for.

keyTerms.meaning: 'She surely weeps': a doubled form of the verb 'to weep'

steps.confusionAlert: This is a new topic. Step 5 has nothing to do with the camel story. The גמרא is returning to the line of explanations of איכה that came before the story.

phrases.english: "She weeps, weeps at night":
phrases.notes: איכה 1:2. The word for weeping is written twice in a row.

phrases.english: Why are there these two weepings?

steps.triggerLanguage: שְׁתֵּי בְּכִיּוֹת הַלָּלוּ לָמָּה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the story and returns to explaining the פסוקים of איכה.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What the doubled verb for weeping in איכה 1:2 is hinting at.

steps.title: Two weepings for the two Temples
steps.stepSummary: רבה, quoting רבי יוחנן, explains that the two weepings are for the first and second בית המקדש.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבה said in the name of רבי יוחנן: One weeping is over the first בית המקדש, and one is over the second בית המקדש.
steps.whatsHappening: רבה, quoting רבי יוחנן, answers the question: each doubled word stands for the loss of one בית המקדש.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The doubled verb is not just style. Each weeping matches one of the two destructions. איכה was written about the first destruction, so this reading has it also weeping ahead of time for the second.

phrases.english: Rabba said that Rabbi Yochanan said:
One is over the First Temple
and one is over the Second Temple.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבָּה אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 5.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The two weepings stand for the destruction of the first and second בית המקדש.

steps.title: "At night" points to the night of the spies
steps.stepSummary: The word 'at night' is explained as weeping over 'matters of the night,' tied to the night the people cried after the report of the מרגלים.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'At night' means the weeping is over matters of the night, as it says: 'And all the congregation lifted up their voice, and the people wept that night.'
steps.whatsHappening: The explanation continues with the next word of the פסוק, 'at night.' It is linked to another פסוק in which the people wept at night.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'At night' is read as pointing to the reason for the weeping, not just the time it happened. The proof פסוק describes the night the people cried over the report of the מרגלים. That earlier crying is linked to the later weeping of איכה.

keyTerms.meaning: Matters of the night, the events connected with a night
As it is said (introduces a proof פסוק)

steps.whatToRemember: Every word of 'בָּכֹה תִבְכֶּה בַּלַּיְלָה' is explained. The doubled weeping is for the two בתי המקדש, and 'at night' links back to the night of crying over the report of the מרגלים.

phrases.english: "At night": over matters of the night,
as it is said:
"And all the congregation lifted up and raised their voice
and the people wept that night."
phrases.notes: במדבר 14:1. This is the night the people cried after hearing the report of the מרגלים.

steps.triggerLanguage: בַּלַּיְלָה עַל עִסְקֵי לַיְלָה שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues explaining the same פסוק, moving on to the word 'at night.'
steps.mimraCoreRuling: 'At night' means weeping over matters of the night, the night the people wept in במדבר 14:1.

steps.title: That night was the night of תשעה באב
steps.stepSummary: רבה in the name of רבי יוחנן says the night ישראל cried over the מרגלים' report was the night of תשעה באב, so ה׳ set a crying for all generations on that date.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבה said in the name of רבי יוחנן: That day was the night of תשעה באב. ה׳ said to ישראל: You cried for no reason, so I will give you a real reason to cry for all generations.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes the idea from the last step. The night ישראל cried after hearing the מרגלים was the night of תשעה באב.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The last step tied 'at night' in איכה to the night of the מרגלים. Now we learn the date: it was תשעה באב. Because they cried for nothing then, that same date became a day of real crying for all generations, which is why both בתי המקדש were destroyed on it.

keyTerms.meaning: The Ninth of Av, the day of mourning for the בית המקדש
Crying for nothing, crying without a real reason

steps.whyThisMatters: This explains why the sad events of Jewish history keep happening on the same date, תשעה באב.

phrases.english: Rabba said that Rabbi Yochanan said:

phrases.aramaic: אוֹתוֹ הַיּוֹם לֵיל תִּשְׁעָה בְּאָב הָיָה.
phrases.english: That day was the night of the Ninth of Av.
phrases.notes: 'That day' means the day the people cried after the מרגלים came back, from the step before.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר לָהֶן הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא לְיִשְׂרָאֵל:
phrases.english: The Holy One, Blessed be He, said to Israel:
You cried a crying for nothing,
and I will set for you a crying for generations.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבָּה אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן: אוֹתוֹ הַיּוֹם לֵיל תִּשְׁעָה בְּאָב הָיָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds the date and the result to the מרגלים explanation of 'at night'.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The crying over the מרגלים happened on the night of תשעה באב, and in return ה׳ made that night a time of crying for all generations.

steps.title: Crying at night is heard
steps.stepSummary: A second explanation of 'at night': whoever cries at night, his voice is heard.
steps.simpleTranslation: Another explanation of 'at night': anyone who cries at night, his voice is heard.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a new and different reason why the פסוק says 'at night'.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Before, 'at night' pointed to a historical night. Here it describes crying itself. At night everything is quiet, so a person's crying carries far and is heard.

phrases.english: Another explanation: "at night":
that anyone who cries at night,
his voice is heard.

steps.triggerLanguage: דָּבָר אַחֵר: ״בַּלַּיְלָה״ – שֶׁכׇּל הַבּוֹכֶה בַּלַּיְלָה, קוֹלוֹ נִשְׁמָע
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a different reading of 'at night' instead of the מרגלים reading.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Crying at night is heard clearly.

steps.title: The stars cry along at night
steps.stepSummary: A third explanation of 'at night': whoever cries at night, the stars and constellations cry with him.
steps.simpleTranslation: Another explanation of 'at night': anyone who cries at night, the stars and constellations cry with him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives one more reason for the word 'at night'.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This time the point is not that people hear the crying. Even the heavens, the stars and constellations, join the crying of a person who weeps at night.

phrases.english: Another explanation: "at night":
that anyone who cries at night,
the stars and constellations cry with him.

steps.triggerLanguage: דָּבָר אַחֵר: ״בַּלַּיְלָה״ – שֶׁכׇּל הַבּוֹכֶה בַּלַּיְלָה, כּוֹכָבִים וּמַזָּלוֹת בּוֹכִין עִמּוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Another separate reading of 'at night'.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The heavens cry along with one who cries at night.

steps.title: Whoever hears night crying cries too
steps.stepSummary: A fourth explanation of 'at night': whoever hears a person crying at night cries along with him.
steps.simpleTranslation: Another explanation of 'at night': anyone who cries at night, whoever hears his voice cries along with him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a last reason for 'at night', and the next step will tell a story to show it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This goes one step past the first explanation. The crying is not only heard; it moves the listener to cry too. That sets up the story of רבן גמליאל.

keyTerms.meaning: Along with him, in response to him

phrases.english: Another explanation: "at night":
that anyone who cries at night,
the one who hears his voice cries along with him.

steps.triggerLanguage: דָּבָר אַחֵר: ״בַּלַּיְלָה״ – שֶׁכׇּל הַבּוֹכֶה בַּלַּיְלָה, הַשּׁוֹמֵעַ קוֹלוֹ בּוֹכֶה כְּנֶגְדּוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A fourth separate reading of 'at night'.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Night crying makes the listener cry too.

steps.title: The story of רבן גמליאל's neighbor
steps.stepSummary: A story shows the last explanation: רבן גמליאל heard his grieving neighbor cry at night and cried with her until his eyelashes fell out.
steps.simpleTranslation: There was a woman, a neighbor of רבן גמליאל, whose son died, and she cried over him at night. רבן גמליאל heard her and cried with her until his eyelashes fell out. The next day his students saw what had happened to him and moved her out of his neighborhood.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a true story to show that a person who hears someone crying at night ends up crying too.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The story backs up the explanation in the step before. רבן גמליאל was so moved by her night crying that it hurt him physically. His students moved her away to protect him.

keyTerms.meaning: A story, an incident that happened

phrases.english: There was an incident with one woman,
the neighbor of Rabban Gamliel,
whose son died,
and she would cry over him at night.
Rabban Gamliel heard her voice
and cried along with her,
until his eyelashes fell out.
The next day his students noticed it on him
and they moved her out of his neighborhood.

steps.triggerLanguage: מַעֲשֶׂה בְּאִשָּׁה אַחַת, שְׁכֶנְתּוֹ שֶׁל רַבָּן גַּמְלִיאֵל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Shows the fourth explanation of 'at night' happening in real life.
steps.raayaObject: That whoever hears crying at night cries along with it.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The story of רבן גמליאל and his grieving neighbor.

steps.title: Tears like a young widow's
steps.stepSummary: רבא in the name of רבי יוחנן says 'her tears are on her cheek' means crying like a woman over the husband of her youth, based on a פסוק in יואל.
steps.simpleTranslation: On the words 'and her tears are on her cheek', רבא said in the name of רבי יוחנן: It is like a woman crying over the husband of her youth, as it says: 'Wail like a young woman wearing sackcloth over the husband of her youth.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to the next phrase in איכה and explains what kind of crying it means.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Tears that stay on the cheek show crying that does not stop. רבי יוחנן compares it to the deepest grief there is: a young wife who lost her husband. The פסוק in יואל supports this picture.

keyTerms.meaning: Wearing sackcloth, a sign of mourning

phrases.english: "And her tears are on her cheek":
phrases.notes: איכה 1:2

phrases.english: Rava said that Rabbi Yochanan said:
Like a woman who cries over the husband of her youth,
as it says: "Wail like a young woman wearing sackcloth
phrases.notes: יואל 1:8

phrases.english: over the husband of her youth."

steps.triggerLanguage: ״וְדִמְעָתָהּ עַל לֶחֱיָהּ״, אָמַר רָבָא אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from 'at night' to the next phrase of the same פסוק.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: ירושלים cries like a young woman who lost her husband.

steps.title: Whoever oppresses Israel becomes a leader
steps.stepSummary: רבא in the name of רבי יוחנן explains 'her enemies became the head': whoever troubles ישראל rises to power, with a פסוק from ישעיהו.
steps.simpleTranslation: On 'her enemies became the head', רבא said in the name of רבי יוחנן: Anyone who troubles ישראל becomes a leader, as it says: 'For there is no weariness for the one who oppresses her. At first He struck lightly the land of זבולון and the land of נפתלי, but later He struck harder, by the way of the sea, across the ירדן, the גליל of the nations.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains another phrase in איכה, saying that enemies of ישראל rise to the top, and brings a פסוק as a source.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The phrase 'became the head' is read as a rule: whoever oppresses ישראל gains power and greatness. The פסוק from ישעיהו describes an enemy who started with a light attack and later struck harder, showing his power kept growing.

phrases.english: "Her enemies became the head":
phrases.notes: איכה 1:5

phrases.english: Rava said that Rabbi Yochanan said:
Anyone who causes distress to Israel becomes a head,

phrases.aramaic: שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר ״כִּי לֹא מוּעָף לַאֲשֶׁר מוּצָק לָהּ
phrases.english: as it says: "For there is no weariness for the one who oppresses her;
phrases.notes: ישעיהו 8:23

phrases.english: at the first time He struck lightly
the land of Zevulun and the land of Naftali,
and the later time He struck heavily

phrases.aramaic: דֶּרֶךְ הַיָּם עֵבֶר הַיַּרְדֵּן גְּלִיל הַגּוֹיִם״.
phrases.english: by the way of the sea, across the Jordan, the Galil of the nations."

steps.triggerLanguage: ״הָיוּ צָרֶיהָ לְרֹאשׁ״, אָמַר רָבָא אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves on to a later phrase in איכה, from a new פסוק.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Whoever troubles ישראל rises to leadership.

steps.title: Oppressors of Israel do not get tired
steps.stepSummary: From the same פסוק in ישעיהו, רבא in the name of רבי יוחנן teaches that whoever oppresses ישראל does not grow tired.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said in the name of רבי יוחנן: Anyone who oppresses ישראל does not grow tired.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא learns a second lesson from the same פסוק it just quoted.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The words 'there is no weariness for the one who oppresses her' are now read on their own. They teach that enemies of ישראל keep their strength and do not get worn out.

phrases.english: Rava said that Rabbi Yochanan said:
Anyone who oppresses Israel does not grow tired.
phrases.notes: This comes from the words 'לא מועף לאשר מוצק לה' at the start of the פסוק just quoted.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רָבָא אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן: כׇּל הַמֵּצִיק לְיִשְׂרָאֵל אֵינוֹ עָיֵף
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws a second lesson from the פסוק in ישעיהו used in the last step.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Oppressors of ישראל do not grow tired.

steps.title: A Torah source for sharing your pain
steps.stepSummary: רבא in the name of רבי יוחנן learns from 'Let it not come to you, all who pass by' that it is proper to tell others about your suffering.
steps.simpleTranslation: On 'Let it not come to you, all who pass by the road', רבא said in the name of רבי יוחנן: From here we have a source in the Torah for complaining about one's troubles to others.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains another phrase in איכה and learns a lesson about how people act when they suffer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: ירושלים calls out to people passing by, telling them about her pain. From this we learn that it is fine to tell others about your suffering, so they will feel for you and pray for you.

keyTerms.meaning: Complaint, crying out about one's troubles
Those who pass by on the road
From the Torah (here meaning from תנ״ך)

phrases.english: "Let it not come to you, all who pass by the road":
phrases.notes: איכה 1:12

phrases.english: Rava said that Rabbi Yochanan said:
From here is a source in the Torah for complaining.
phrases.notes: Complaining here means telling people about your pain so they will feel for you.

steps.confusionAlert: 'Complaining' here is not a bad thing. It means sharing your suffering with others so they will care for you.
steps.triggerLanguage: ״לֹא אֲלֵיכֶם כׇּל עֹבְרֵי דֶרֶךְ״, אָמַר רָבָא אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן: מִכָּאן לְקוּבְלָנָא מִן הַתּוֹרָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves on to a later פסוק in איכה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: It is proper to tell others about your suffering.

steps.title: Jerusalem was treated like lawbreakers
steps.stepSummary: רב reads 'all who pass by the road' as a hint to 'those who break the law': ירושלים says she was treated like the worst sinners.
steps.simpleTranslation: On 'all who pass by the road', רב עמרם said in the name of רב: They made me like those who break the law.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a second reading of the same words, 'all who pass by', and the next step will bring the proof.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב plays on the words: 'passing by the road' sounds like 'passing over the law', meaning breaking it. ירושלים is crying that she was punished like a city of total lawbreakers.

keyTerms.meaning: They made me, they treated me as

phrases.english: "All who pass by the road":
Rav Amram said that Rav said:
They made me like those who break the law.
phrases.notes: A play on words: 'עוברי דרך' (passing by the road) is read as 'עוברי על דת' (breaking the law). ירושלים is the one speaking.

steps.triggerLanguage: ״כׇּל עֹבְרֵי דֶרֶךְ״, אָמַר רַב עַמְרָם אָמַר רַב: עֲשָׂאוּנִי כְּעוֹבְרֵי עַל דָּת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second reading of the same words from the previous step.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: ירושלים was punished like a city of lawbreakers.

steps.title: Proof: fire from heaven on both Sodom and Jerusalem
steps.stepSummary: The proof for רב: both סדום and ירושלים had fire sent down from heaven, and a פסוק says ירושלים's sin was greater than סדום's.
steps.simpleTranslation: For about סדום it is written: 'And ה׳ rained upon סדום', and about ירושלים it is written: 'From above He sent fire into my bones, and it overcame them.' And it is written: 'The sin of the daughter of my people is greater than the sin of סדום.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא proves רב's point that ירושלים was treated like the lawbreakers of סדום.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The only city famous for fire from heaven was סדום, the city of lawbreakers. ירושלים also got fire from above, so she was treated like סדום. The last פסוק explains why: ירושלים's sin was even greater than סדום's.

keyTerms.meaning: The wicked city destroyed in the days of אברהם

steps.whatToRemember: The פסוקים of איכה are explained phrase by phrase: the crying at night, the young widow's tears, the rise of ישראל's enemies, the source for sharing pain, and ירושלים punished like סדום because her sin was greater.

phrases.english: For regarding Sodom it is written:
"And ה׳ rained upon Sodom,"
phrases.notes: בראשית 19:24

phrases.english: while regarding Jerusalem it is written:
"From above He sent fire into my bones, and it overcame them, etc."
phrases.notes: איכה 1:13

phrases.aramaic: וּכְתִיב: ״וַיִּגְדַּל עֲוֹן בַּת עַמִּי מֵחַטַּאת סְדֹם״.
phrases.english: And it is written: "The sin of the daughter of my people is greater than the sin of Sodom."
phrases.notes: איכה 4:6

steps.triggerLanguage: דְּאִילּוּ בִּסְדוֹם כְּתִיב: ״וַה׳ הִמְטִיר עַל סְדֹם״
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings פסוקים to prove רב's statement.
steps.raayaObject: That ירושלים was treated like the lawbreakers of סדום.

steps.title: Why was ירושלים treated more gently than סדום?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the previous step: if ירושלים's sin was greater, why was it not overturned like סדום? Is there favoritism?
steps.simpleTranslation: Is there favoritism here? If ירושלים sinned more, why wasn't it overturned like סדום?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא raises a challenge against the proof it just brought. If ירושלים sinned more than סדום, it seems unfair that סדום got the harsher punishment.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 18 used a פסוק saying ירושלים's sin was greater than סדום's, and that same פסוק says סדום was overturned in a moment. If ירושלים was worse, it should have been punished at least as harshly. Saying ה׳ went easier on ירושלים would mean ה׳ shows favoritism, which cannot be.

keyTerms.meaning: Favoritism, literally 'lifting the face' of someone to treat them better
'And is it so that...?', a word that opens a doubtful question

phrases.english: And is there favoritism in the matter?
phrases.notes: The rest of that פסוק (איכה 4:6) says סדום was overturned in a moment. So why wasn't ירושלים, if its sin was greater?

steps.triggerLanguage: וְכִי מַשּׂוֹא פָּנִים יֵשׁ בַּדָּבָר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the proof brought in step 18
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim in step 18 that ירושלים's sin was greater than סדום's, given that סדום got the harsher punishment
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A greater sin should bring an equal or greater punishment. If ירושלים got a lighter punishment, it looks like favoritism, which cannot be said about ה׳.

steps.title: ירושלים suffered an extra measure that סדום never had
steps.stepSummary: רבא in the name of רבי יוחנן answers that ירושלים was punished with extra suffering. סדום had plenty of bread, while in ירושלים the famine was so terrible that mothers cooked their own children.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said in the name of רבי יוחנן: ירושלים had an extra measure of suffering that סדום did not have. About סדום it says they had plenty of bread. But about ירושלים it says that compassionate women cooked their own children.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא in the name of רבי יוחנן answers the challenge. ירושלים was not treated more gently. It actually suffered a terrible extra punishment, a famine, that סדום never went through.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The question assumed that sudden destruction is the worst punishment. The answer shows that ירושלים's slow, starving suffering was in some ways worse than סדום's quick end. סדום is described with 'plenty of bread', so they never knew hunger, while ירושלים reached a famine so terrible that mothers cooked their children. So there was no favoritism: ירושלים's greater sin brought a different and very heavy punishment.

keyTerms.meaning: An extra measure, here meaning an extra measure of suffering
Plenty of bread, being full and well-fed

steps.whyThisMatters: It removes the idea of favoritism and shows that a quick punishment is not always the harsher one.

phrases.english: Rava said that Rabbi Yochanan said:
There was an extra measure in Jerusalem
phrases.notes: He means an extra measure of suffering.

phrases.english: that was not in Sodom,
for regarding Sodom it is written:
"Behold, this was the sin of your sister Sodom:
pride, plenty of bread

phrases.aramaic: וְיַד עָנִי וְאֶבְיוֹן לֹא הֶחֱזִיקָה וְגוֹ׳״,
phrases.english: and she did not strengthen the hand of the poor and needy, etc."
phrases.notes: יחזקאל 16:49

phrases.english: whereas regarding Jerusalem it is written:
"The hands of compassionate women
cooked their children."
phrases.notes: איכה 4:10

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רָבָא אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן: מִדָּה יְתֵירָה הָיְתָה בִּירוּשָׁלַיִם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of favoritism raised in step 19
steps.terutzResolutionType: Redefines which punishment was really harsher
steps.terutzHavaAmina: ירושלים got off lighter because it was not overturned in a moment like סדום
steps.terutzMaskana: ירושלים suffered an extra measure, a terrible famine, that סדום never had, so there was no favoritism

steps.title: The mighty ones of ירושלים became like an invalid coin
steps.stepSummary: The word סלה in the פסוק is read like נפסלה, 'invalidated'. The leaders of ירושלים lost their worth, like a coin that is no longer accepted.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'ה׳ has spurned all my mighty ones in my midst' is like a person who tells his friend: this coin has been invalidated.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves on to explain another פסוק in איכה. It compares the fall of ירושלים's great people to a coin that has been taken out of use.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word סִלָּה sounds like נִפְסְלָה, 'became invalid'. A canceled coin may look the same, but it no longer has any value. In the same way, the important people of ירושלים lost all their standing and respect.

keyTerms.meaning: Spurned or trampled, read here like 'invalidated'
My mighty ones, the strong and important people
A coin has been invalidated and can no longer be used

phrases.english: "The Lord has spurned all my mighty ones in my midst,"
phrases.notes: איכה 1:15. The word סלה is being read like נפסלה, 'invalidated'.

phrases.english: like a person who says to his friend:
This coin has been invalidated.

steps.triggerLanguage: סִלָּה כׇל אַבִּירַי ה׳ בְּקִרְבִּי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves on from the סדום comparison to explain the next פסוק in איכה
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The leaders of ירושלים lost their worth like a coin that has been taken out of use

steps.title: Why פ comes before ע in איכה: the מרגלים
steps.stepSummary: רבא in the name of רבי יוחנן explains why some chapters of איכה put the פ verse before the ע verse. It is because of the מרגלים, who said with their mouth (פה) what they did not see with their eyes (עין).
steps.simpleTranslation: 'They opened their mouths against you.' רבא said in the name of רבי יוחנן: Why was פ put before ע? Because of the spies, who said with their mouths what they had not seen with their eyes.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא in the name of רבי יוחנן explains a puzzle in the alphabet order of איכה. He links it to the sin of the מרגלים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Some chapters of איכה follow the alphabet, and normally ע comes before פ. Here the order is switched. פ stands for פה, 'mouth', and ע for עין, 'eye', so putting the mouth before the eye hints at the מרגלים, who spoke a bad report before actually seeing anything.

keyTerms.meaning: The spies משה sent to the land of Israel

steps.confusionAlert: In the alphabet ע comes before פ. The question is why איכה switches them, not why פ comes first in general.

phrases.english: "They opened their mouths against you" –
phrases.notes: איכה 2:16. This פסוק starts with פ and comes before the one starting with ע.

phrases.english: Rava said that Rabbi Yochanan said:
For what reason did he put פ before ע?
Because of the spies
who said with their mouths
what they did not see with their eyes.
phrases.notes: פה means mouth and עין means eye, so the letters hint at mouth before eyes.

steps.triggerLanguage: בִּשְׁבִיל מָה הִקְדִּים פֵּא לְעַיִן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues explaining פסוקים from איכה
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The letter פ comes before ע in איכה to hint at the מרגלים, who spoke before they saw

steps.title: Israel's enemies only enjoy the bread of ישראל
steps.stepSummary: On the פסוק 'those who eat My people ate bread', רבא in the name of רבי יוחנן teaches that those who rob ישראל only really taste bread when it comes from ישראל.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'Those who eat My people ate bread, they did not call upon ה׳.' רבא said in the name of רבי יוחנן: Whoever eats the bread of ישראל tastes the taste of bread. Whoever does not eat from the bread of ישראל does not taste the taste of bread.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a פסוק from תהלים about those who 'eat' ישראל. רבא in the name of רבי יוחנן explains that these enemies only enjoy food that they take from ישראל.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק joins 'eating My people' with 'eating bread'. רבי יוחנן reads this to mean that for these enemies, bread only has real taste when it is taken from ישראל. Their own food gives them no satisfaction.

keyTerms.meaning: Those who 'eat' My people, those who rob and devour ישראל
Tastes the taste of bread, really enjoys the food
The bread of the Jewish people

phrases.english: "Those who eat My people ate bread,
they did not call upon the Lord."
phrases.notes: תהלים 14:4

phrases.english: Rava said that Rabbi Yochanan said:
Anyone who eats from the bread of the Jewish people
tastes the taste of bread,
and one who does not eat from the bread of the Jewish people
does not taste the taste of bread.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֹכְלֵי עַמִּי אָכְלוּ לֶחֶם ה׳ לֹא קָרָאוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the series of רבא in the name of רבי יוחנן teachings about those who oppress ישראל
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Those who rob ישראל only enjoy the taste of bread when it comes from ישראל

steps.title: Who 'did not call upon ה׳': judges or teachers?
steps.stepSummary: רב and שמואל argue about who the end of the פסוק refers to. רב says it means judges, and שמואל says it means teachers of young children.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'They did not call upon ה׳': רב says these are the judges, and שמואל says these are the teachers of young children.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains the second half of the same פסוק. רב and שמואל each say who it is talking about.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The phrase 'they did not call upon ה׳' is read as describing people in an important role who do not do it for the sake of Heaven. רב says it means judges, and שמואל says it means teachers of children. Both pick a job that is supposed to be done in ה׳'s name.
steps.whatToRemember: ירושלים was not treated with favoritism: it suffered a terrible famine that סדום never knew. Then the גמרא explained several פסוקים: the fallen leaders were like an invalid coin, פ before ע hints at the מרגלים, enemies only enjoy ישראל's bread, and רב and שמואל argue whether 'they did not call upon ה׳' means judges or teachers.

phrases.english: "They did not call upon the Lord" –
Rav says: These are the judges,
and Shmuel says: These are the teachers of young children.

steps.triggerLanguage: ה׳ לֹא קָרָאוּ – רַב אָמַר: אֵלּוּ הַדַּיָּינִין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the second half of the פסוק quoted in step 23
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רב: 'they did not call upon ה׳' refers to judges. שמואל: it refers to teachers of young children.

steps.title: Who made the list?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks who listed the kings and commoners in the משנה who have no share in עולם הבא.
steps.simpleTranslation: Who counted them?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back to the list in the משנה and asks who put it together. This question sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה named kings and commoners who lose עולם הבא. A list that serious needs someone with authority behind it, so the גמרא asks who that was.

phrases.english: Who counted them?
phrases.notes: "Them" means the kings and commoners listed in the משנה as having no share in עולם הבא.

steps.triggerLanguage: מִי מְנָאָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the aggadic teachings on איכה and returns to the list in the משנה.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Who had the authority to make the list of those with no share in עולם הבא.

steps.title: The אנשי כנסת הגדולה made the list
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי answers that the אנשי כנסת הגדולה counted them.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אשי said: The men of the Great Assembly counted them.
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי answers the question. The list was made by the אנשי כנסת הגדולה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The list comes from the great court of early בית שני times, so it carries real authority. This also sets up the next story about how they wanted to add one more name.

keyTerms.meaning: the Men of the Great Assembly, the leading sages at the start of בית שני

phrases.english: Rav Ashi said:
The men of the Great Assembly counted them.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב אָשֵׁי אַנְשֵׁי כְּנֶסֶת הַגְּדוֹלָה מְנָאוּם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 25.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The אנשי כנסת הגדולה made the list.

steps.title: They wanted to add one more king, and ignored signs from heaven
steps.stepSummary: רב says the אנשי כנסת הגדולה wanted to add one more king. The image of his father bowed before them and a fire burned their benches, but they paid no attention.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יהודה said in the name of רב: They wanted to count one more. The image of his father's face came and bowed down in front of them, and they paid no attention to it. A fire came down from heaven and licked at their benches, and they paid no attention to it.
steps.whatsHappening: רב tells a story. The sages wanted to add one more king to the list, and two signs from heaven tried to stop them, but they ignored both.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The king is not named here, but the next step shows it is שלמה, and the 'father' is דוד. First דוד's image begs for his son, then a fire threatens the sages. They stay firm, which shows they thought they were judging correctly.

keyTerms.meaning: bowed down, lay down flat (to plead)

steps.confusionAlert: The sages are not being rebellious for no reason. They believed שלמה's sins deserved it, so they did not let signs change a judgment they thought was right.

phrases.english: Rav Yehuda said in the name of Rav:
They wanted to count one more.
The image of the face of his father came
phrases.notes: His father is דוד המלך.

phrases.english: and bowed down before them,
and they paid no attention to it.
A fire came from heaven
and (the fire) licked at their benches,
phrases.notes: Some versions leave out the word in round brackets; the meaning stays the same.

phrases.english: and they paid no attention to it.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב יְהוּדָה אָמַר רַב בִּקְּשׁוּ עוֹד לִמְנוֹת אֶחָד
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Builds on step 26: the same אנשי כנסת הגדולה tried to add another name.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The אנשי כנסת הגדולה wanted to add שלמה to the list and ignored two heavenly signs against it.

steps.title: A בת קול praises שלמה for building the בית המקדש first
steps.stepSummary: A בת קול quotes a פסוק in משלי to praise שלמה, who built the בית המקדש before his own palace and faster. The sages still paid no attention.
steps.simpleTranslation: A בת קול came out and said to them: 'Do you see a man quick in his work? He will stand before kings, he will not stand before lowly people.' This is someone who put My house before his own house. Not only that, he built My house in seven years and his own house in thirteen years. 'He will stand before kings, he will not stand before lowly people.' And he paid no attention to it.
steps.whatsHappening: A voice from heaven now speaks openly in שלמה's defense. The sages still do not listen.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The בת קול points to a real merit: שלמה gave priority to הקב״ה's house over his own. He built the בית המקדש quickly, in seven years, but took thirteen years for his palace. A man like that belongs 'before kings', not on a list of the wicked.

keyTerms.meaning: quick and skilled in his work

phrases.english: A Divine Voice came out and said to them:
"Do you see a man quick in his work?
phrases.notes: משלי 22:29

phrases.english: He will stand before kings,
he will not stand before lowly people."
One who put My house before his house,
phrases.notes: "My house" is the בית המקדש, and "his house" is שלמה's palace.

phrases.aramaic: וְלֹא עוֹד אֶלָּא שֶׁבֵּיתִי בָּנָה בְּשֶׁבַע שָׁנִים
phrases.english: and not only that, but My house he built in seven years
and his house he built in thirteen years.
"He will stand before kings,
[he will not stand] before lowly people."
phrases.notes: Some versions don't have the words in square brackets; the corrected wording adds them to finish the פסוק.

phrases.english: And he paid no attention to it.
phrases.notes: Written in the singular. It most likely means the court as one group.

steps.triggerLanguage: יָצְאָה בַּת קוֹל וְאָמְרָה לָהֶם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: The third and strongest sign, after the image and the fire in step 27.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: שלמה's merit of building the בית המקדש before his palace makes him worthy to 'stand before kings'.

steps.title: Only הקב״ה decides who gets reward
steps.stepSummary: A second בת קול quotes איוב: is reward handed out by your choice? It is הקב״ה's decision, not yours. So שלמה was left off the list.
steps.simpleTranslation: A בת קול came out and said: 'Should He pay reward according to you, because you have rejected? Will you choose and not I?' and so on.
steps.whatsHappening: The final בת קול ends the story. It tells the sages that deciding who gets עולם הבא is not up to them.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The earlier signs argued about whether שלמה deserved it. This last voice moves the question to who has the right to decide, and the answer is only הקב״ה. That is why שלמה does not appear in the משנה's list.

keyTerms.meaning: He will pay it back, give reward

steps.whatToRemember: The list was made by the אנשי כנסת הגדולה, but they were stopped from adding שלמה, because only הקב״ה decides who has a share in עולם הבא.

phrases.english: A Divine Voice came out and said:
"Shall He pay it according to you, because you have rejected?
phrases.notes: איוב 34:33

phrases.aramaic: כִּי אַתָּה תִבְחַר וְלֹא אֲנִי וְגוֹ׳״.
phrases.english: For you will choose and not I? and so on."

steps.triggerLanguage: יָצְאָה בַּת קוֹל וְאָמְרָה הַמֵעִמְּךָ יְשַׁלְמֶנָּה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Ends the story with a final statement after the sages ignored step 28.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Reward in עולם הבא is decided by הקב״ה alone, so שלמה was not added to the list.

steps.title: The דורשי רשומות: all of them come to עולם הבא
steps.stepSummary: The דורשי רשומות say that everyone on the list does come to עולם הבא, and they bring a פסוק in תהלים.
steps.simpleTranslation: The interpreters of hints used to say: All of them come to עולם הבא, as it says: 'Gilead is Mine and Menashe is Mine, and Ephraim is the strength of My head, Yehuda is My lawgiver. Moav is My washing pot, on Edom I will throw My shoe, Philistia, shout because of Me.'
steps.whatsHappening: A new group with a surprising view comes in. They say everyone on the משנה's list ends up in עולם הבא, and they quote a פסוק as their source.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This goes directly against the plain meaning of the משנה. Their proof is a פסוק they read as hidden hints, where הקב״ה says 'Mine' about names that stand for the wicked kings. The next step starts explaining each hint.

keyTerms.meaning: those who read hidden hints in the פסוקים

steps.confusionAlert: This is the opinion of a specific group of דרשנים. It is not the ruling of the משנה, which says these people have no share.

phrases.english: The interpreters of hints used to say:

steps.triggerLanguage: דּוֹרְשֵׁי רְשׁוּמוֹת הָיוּ אוֹמְרִים כּוּלָּן בָּאִין לָעוֹלָם הַבָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the story of the list, brings a group who say that everyone on the list ends up in עולם הבא.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: According to the דורשי רשומות, all those listed come to עולם הבא, based on a פסוק in תהלים.

steps.title: Reading the פסוק: אחאב, מנשה, ירבעם, אחיתופל
steps.stepSummary: The דורשי רשומות match each part of the פסוק to a person on the list: Gilead is אחאב, Menashe is מנשה, Ephraim is ירבעם, and Yehuda is אחיתופל.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'Gilead is Mine': this is אחאב, who fell at רמות גלעד. 'Menashe': as it sounds. 'Ephraim is the strength of My head': this is ירבעם, who came from אפרים. 'Yehuda is My lawgiver': this is אחיתופל.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains the פסוק piece by piece, showing which wicked person each name hints to. The list continues past this point.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each link is made through a place or a tribe. אחאב died at רמות גלעד, ירבעם was from the tribe of אפרים, and מנשה is simply named. Since הקב״ה says 'Mine' about each of them, the דורשי רשומות read it as bringing them close in the end.
